archetype.name: Playoff Team (structure-first)
archetype.definition: A Vegas team whose record rests on keeping shots and chances against down, with a deep center group and a steady goalie tandem doing the rest, rather than on hot finishing or close-game luck.

report.headline: Vegas is winning on structure, not luck, though the margin was built early.
report.take:
Vegas at 12-5-2 is fifth on the site's Teams tab and second in the Pacific behind Edmonton. The profile is honest. They are fifth in goals allowed per game (2.68), allow 25.7 shots a game against a league average of 27, and own a 52.8% expected-goals share at 5-on-5, tenth in the league. The offense is merely good: 3.37 goals a game, 12th. This isn't a run-and-gun team. It controls the slot, lets its centers drive play, and trusts two goalies who have both been above expected.

What's driving it is depth down the middle. Jack Eichel (24 points, 11th on the centers tab) carries the top line, and Tomas Hertl has been one of the league's best centers on a per-minute basis: 9 goals, a 63% xGF and sixth on his tab while playing only 15.38 minutes a night. Mark Stone's 10 goals put him third among right wingers. The defense has been just as good against opposing centers: Vegas has held them further under their expected output than any team in the league, and second-best against forwards overall. The power play (26.3%, ninth) adds an edge that has been a fixture since 2024-25.

The luck indicators are quiet, and that is the good news. Pts vs Goal Diff sits at +0.7, 5-on-5 PDO at 100.6, and the skaters' 11.6% shooting is exactly league average. The one place Vegas is running above the field is in net. Its .902 save percentage ranks seventh against a .891 league mark, and that is a real change from last season's -16.5 GSAx. What the season numbers do hide is timing. Over the last 10 games Vegas is 5-3-2 with a -1 goal differential, scoring 0.57 goals a game below its season rate. Three blowout losses in October to Tampa, St. Louis and New Jersey sit inside that stretch. The most recent five have been tighter and more like the team's identity: 2.4 goals allowed a game and a 3-1-1 record.

The direction is still up. Vegas's goal differential per game (0.68) matches the 2024-25 team that finished with 110 points, and the full-season pace is 112. The chance share is better than that 2024-25 team's. Mitch Marner has 3 goals on 41 shots, which leaves room for more finishing. If the goaltending merely holds around average, this is a top-three Pacific team with a real case for the division.

strengths.title: Suppression built around centers
strengths.body: Vegas gives up few shots and few good ones, and opposing centers produce well under their norms against it. It is the league's best team by that measure, and second-best against all forwards. That kind of positional defense comes from structure and center depth rather than bounces, so it should hold up over a season.

strengths.title: Hertl and Eichel driving the middle
strengths.body: Eichel's 24 points lead the team, and Hertl's 63% xGF in third-line minutes gives Vegas a second center who wins his matchups outright. Stone's 10 goals finish what they create. The A- forward grade is spread across several players instead of resting on one, which makes it sturdier.

strengths.title: Two goalies above expected
strengths.body: Hill (+2.3 GSAx) and Hart (+1.7) have split the starts almost evenly, and both have saved more than an average goalie would have. Last year the crease cost Vegas 16.5 goals against expected. Neither save percentage is extreme, so this looks like competence rather than a heater, though it is the stat most likely to drift.

concerns.title: The margin has gone flat lately
concerns.body: Vegas has been outscored over its last 10 games, and its scoring rate in that stretch is well below the season mark. The three October blowouts account for much of that. November has been tight and low-scoring, which fits the team's style. Still, the impressive season differential was mostly banked in the first few weeks.

concerns.title: An ordinary penalty kill
concerns.body: At 76.5%, the PK ranks 17th and sits slightly below the league average. That fits Vegas's history: it has hovered in the mid-to-high 70s for years, apart from last season's 81.4%. It is not a crisis, but it is the soft spot a strong power play can exploit.

concerns.title: Second-pair blueline is underwater
concerns.body: Theodore and McNabb are excellent, both above 60% xGF. Behind them, Andersson, Hanifin and Lauzon are all at or below even in chance share, while playing heavy minutes. That is why the defense grades a B while the forwards grade A-, and the gap will matter against teams with real depth.

trend.note: A fast start built the differential, and a rough late-October patch flattened it. November has brought the team back to low-event hockey and wins, with only seven goals allowed in four games.

weekAhead.headline: Three home games, two leaky goaltending teams and Nashville
weekAhead.body:
All three games are at home, and two of the opponents rank near the bottom in goaltending. Utah is the most dangerous: it has the league's second-best xGF share and power play, but its goalies are 30th in save percentage. Vegas's tight checking should be able to cash in on that. Nashville is the opposite: a team getting outshot that survives on goaltending, an elite PK and close-game points. Vancouver is last on the site, allows the most to forwards of any team and stops .859 of its shots.

Two wins is the floor here and three is realistic. The Nashville game is the one where Vegas's chance edge may not show up on the scoreboard.

keyMatchups.title: Vegas PK vs Utah power play
keyMatchups.body: Utah converts 37.1% of its power plays, second in the league, against a Vegas kill that ranks 17th. Staying out of the box is the clearest way to blunt Utah's best weapon. On the other end, Utah's 27th-ranked PK gives Vegas's ninth-ranked power play a target.

keyMatchups.title: Nashville's goaltending vs Vegas's chances
keyMatchups.body: Nashville owns only 45% of 5-on-5 shot attempts, 28th in the league, yet its goalies are 6.9 goals above expected and its PK ranks third. Vegas should control play. Whether that becomes goals depends on beating a goalie who has bailed Nashville out all year.

keyMatchups.title: Vancouver's open door for forwards
keyMatchups.body: Vancouver's forwards-allowed number is the worst in the league, with wingers in particular scoring far above their norms. Add a .859 save percentage, and this is a spot for Stone, Marner and Connelly to pad totals. Marner's low goal count in particular could get a lift here.

weekAhead.watch: Whether Vegas's scoring rebounds against two bottom-tier goaltending teams, or the low-output November trend continues.

restOfSeason.body:
Very little of Vegas's record depends on luck. Close-game points, 5-on-5 PDO and shooting percentage all sit near average, and the chance share supports a top-10 team. The 112-point pace is plausible, but it needs the goaltending to stay above average. That is the shakiest piece, given last year's crease. A realistic range is 102 to 112 points and 46 to 52 wins, enough to challenge Edmonton for the Pacific. The goal differential per game should settle somewhere between 0.4 and 0.7 as the blowout-heavy October stretch averages out.

The upside comes from the forward group: Marner's finishing should improve, and Hertl's play has been strong enough to hold. The downside comes from the blueline behind the top pair, and from regression in net if Hill and Hart slip back toward average or worse.
swingFactors: Whether Hill and Hart stay above expected
Depth defense behind Theodore and McNabb
Marner's finishing catching up to his chances

confidence.note: 19 games is a small sample, but the underlying numbers and history point the same way.
